title: Crowd-pleasing cost of living measures risk being self-defeating
gist: Resolution Foundation (Ruth Curtice, James Smith) warns that unfunded, universal cost of living support in the upcoming UK Budget could backfire by pushing up Bank of England rates and mortgage costs and by creating an inflation cliff when temporary measures like the energy VAT cut expire. It argues instead for fully funded, targeted measures: a £2bn income-tested energy bill scheme, relinking Local Housing Allowance to rents, and a low-cost Starter Deposit Scheme.

themes.theme: UK fiscal squeeze before the Budget

insights.claim: Higher global government borrowing costs alone are expected to cost the UK Chancellor over £10 billion in the upcoming Budget forecast, with Middle East conflict further deteriorating the public finances outlook.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Limited fiscal headroom raises the odds of tax rises or spending restraint in the UK Budget; watch gilt yields and OBR forecast revisions.
insights.quote: the increase in the cost of government borrowing alone costing him over £10 billion
insights.locator: The outlook ahead of the Budget is bleak

insights.claim: Andy Burnham's government has already introduced a possibly temporary VAT cut on energy bills and admitted more cost of living support is needed, raising expectations for further announcements as wholesale energy prices peak again.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Political pressure for giveaways ahead of the Budget is a source of UK fiscal and gilt risk.

insights.claim: Debt-funded cost of living support adds to demand during high inflation, pushing up Bank of England short-term rates and therefore mortgage rates, which offsets the direct relief to consumers.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Unfunded UK fiscal loosening should be read as hawkish for BoE rate expectations and bearish for gilts and mortgage-sensitive sectors like housebuilders.

insights.claim: HM Treasury has previously estimated that additional borrowing of 1% of GDP (around £30bn) can raise UK short-term interest rates by 50 to 125 basis points.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A usable rule of thumb to translate UK Budget borrowing surprises into front-end rate moves (SONIA/short sterling).
insights.quote: additional borrowing of 1 per cent of GDP – around £30bn – can increase rates in the short-term by 50 to 125bps
insights.locator: Indeed, the Treasury has previously estimated

insights.claim: A global price shock with little spare capacity in the UK economy, combined with sovereign debt market wobbles, is precisely the setting in which extra government borrowing does more harm than good, so any new support must be fully funded.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Markets are likely to punish an unfunded UK package; a fully funded one reduces gilt tail risk.
insights.quote: In short, fresh support must be fully funded.

insights.claim: Temporary price-lowering measures such as a VAT cut reduce measured inflation for a year but create upward inflation pressure when removed, which can delay the return of UK inflation to target.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Expect a base-effect inflation spike when the energy VAT cut ends; fade arguments that fiscal inflation-reducing measures justify earlier BoE cuts.
insights.quote: If support is temporary then it will lead to upward pressure on inflation when it is removed.

insights.claim: Some Monetary Policy Committee members suggest headline inflation may influence second-round wage effects, making headline-lowering fiscal measures temporarily relevant to rate decisions, unlike in normal times.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Watch MPC commentary on second-round effects; headline CPI moves driven by fiscal measures may matter more for BoE pricing than usual.
insights.locator: In normal times this would not

insights.claim: A universal VAT cut on energy bills spreads support thinly and gives better-off households more cash than poorer ones, even though bills are a far larger share of poorer households' budgets.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Universal energy measures are poor value per pound of borrowing, strengthening the case for replacing them with targeted schemes.
insights.quote: better off households will actually gain more in cash terms
insights.locator: The VAT cut on electricity bills

insights.claim: Resolution Foundation proposes a £2bn energy support scheme for households where no one earns over £24,000, reaching two in five households and three-quarters of the poorest four income deciles, paying £220 below £18,000 income and £85 above.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A benchmark for what a targeted, costed Budget energy package could look like and its fiscal size.

insights.claim: Targeted energy support could be kept temporary by making it expressly triggered by the energy price cap exceeding a particular high level.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A price-cap-linked trigger would tie UK fiscal costs directly to wholesale gas/power prices.

insights.claim: Relinking Local Housing Allowance to the 30th percentile of local rents would be the most powerful single measure for lower-income households, costing £2.5bn in 2029-30, with the typical two-bedroom shortfall now about £160 a month and set to hit a record this autumn.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: An LHA relink would boost rental income security for landlords serving benefit claimants and support low-income consumption.
insights.locator: Beyond action on bills, the most

insights.claim: An LHA relink could be funded within the working-age welfare budget by raising the Universal Credit taper from 55% to 59%.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Signals a fiscally neutral redistribution option within welfare, reducing work incentives slightly for UC claimants.

insights.claim: A well-targeted Starter Deposit Scheme could help younger families get onto the housing ladder at negligible fiscal cost.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A potential Budget measure supportive of first-time buyer demand, relevant to UK housebuilders and mortgage lenders.
